750.title: Pandu's message
750.hook: a father among the dead asks his son for a deed; why Hindus still make offerings for their ancestors
750.carry: what we do still reaches the ancestors
750.howItsDone: Hindu families honor their ancestors in shraddha rites, with offerings of rice (pinda), sesame and water, and in Pitru Paksha, the fortnight when the ancestors are remembered together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sabha heard about the halls of the gods, and a guardian for every direction. Your line was lokapalas: every direction has a guardian.

Yudhishthira has been listening closely, and he's noticed something. In Indra's hall, among all the sages and gods, Narada named only one human king: Harishchandra. Not the great kings of Yudhishthira's own line, not the heroes of the old stories. One name. Why him? the king asks. And there's a second question underneath. In Yama's hall, among the dead, you saw my father. You saw Pandu. What did he say?
screen: `ONE KING IN INDRA'S HALL.` → `WHY HARISHCHANDRA?` → `AND MY FATHER?`

segments.voice: Narada answers the first question first. Harishchandra was a mighty king who brought other kings under him and then performed the great sacrifice called the Rajasuya. He gave generously to everyone who came, and because of that sacrifice, he shines in Indra's hall. Then the second answer. Narada had seen Pandu in Yama's hall, and Pandu had seen Harishchandra's place. So Pandu gave Narada a message. Tell my son: you are able to conquer the earth, and your brothers obey you. Perform the Rajasuya. Then I, and our ancestors, may go to Indra's world. Sit with that. Yudhishthira's father died when the brothers were young, and now, in the brand-new hall, a sage delivers his words. Not comfort. A request, and a heavy one: do this, so that I, and the fathers before me, can rise. That isn't only Pandu's wish. It's one of Hinduism's oldest ideas. The living and the ancestors, the pitris, stay tied together, and what the living do can still reach them. Old Vedic texts say every person is born owing three debts: to the gods, to the sages who taught, and to the ancestors. That last debt is paid by carrying the family on, and by honoring the dead in shraddha: offerings of rice, sesame and water, made for the dead by name, often by a son, just as Pandu turns to his eldest. Every year, in the fortnight called Pitru Paksha, many Hindu families do it together. Many teachers read it simply: love doesn't stop at death. Tomorrow, Narada adds something far less welcome.
screen: `HARISHCHANDRA'S SACRIFICE.` · `TELL MY SON: PERFORM THE RAJASUYA.` · `THE PITRIS, STILL TIED TO US.` · `THREE DEBTS, AND SHRADDHA.` · then, large: `LOVE DOESN'T STOP AT DEATH.`

segments.voice: If your family keeps Pitru Paksha or shraddha, this is a small version of it. Pour a little water into a cup or onto a plant, and as you pour, say the name of someone in your family who has died, a grandparent or someone further back, and thank them for one thing that reached you. If you pray, offer the water to them and to God. If you don't, just say the name and the thank you, and let the water go.

751.title: Send for Krishna
751.hook: everyone in the hall says yes, and Yudhishthira still sends for Krishna, the friend who sees further
751.carry: krishna, the friend who sees further

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pandu's words, carried by Narada, asking his son to perform the Rajasuya. Your line was what we do still reaches the ancestors.
screen: `WHAT WE DO STILL REACHES THE ANCESTORS.`

segments.voice: Narada has one more thing to say before he goes. This sacrifice, he tells the king, is hard to finish. It has many obstacles. Brahma-rakshasas, demons who haunt sacrifices, look for any flaw in it. And after it, a war can come that destroys the warriors of the earth. Think it over, Narada says. Do what's good for you. Then he leaves, and the hall is left holding both halves of the message.
screen: `HARD TO FINISH.` → `DEMONS LOOK FOR FLAWS.` → `A WAR CAN COME AFTER.`

segments.voice: A dead father asking his son to rise to this. A sage warning that it might end in ruin. Yudhishthira brushes aside neither. The text says he sighed, and thought, and couldn't find peace. So he asks. First his ministers and his brothers: you deserve this, they say, do it. Then the priests and sages, Dhaumya, and Vyasa himself. They agree too. Everyone in the room says yes. And still Yudhishthira doesn't move. People who love you, he reasons, don't always point out the danger. Some say what pleases. So he thinks of the one who won't flatter him and sees further than anyone: Krishna. He sends a fast messenger to Dwaraka, and Krishna comes quickly. Here's why that matters to Hindus. Krishna isn't just a clever cousin. Many Hindus worship him as God himself, Vishnu come into the world, and the Mahabharata keeps showing him in one role above all: the friend at your side who sees what you can't. Devotees even have a name for loving God this way: sakhya, friendship, one of the moods of bhakti. Watch for it. Later in this serial, on a battlefield, Arjuna will turn to the same friend in his worst hour, and what Krishna says there becomes the Bhagavad Gita. Today is the small first version: a good king, surrounded by yeses, who still wants Krishna's eyes on it. Many Hindus still bring a big choice to God first, at the home shrine or the temple, before they decide. Tomorrow, Krishna answers.
screen: `A REQUEST AND A WARNING.` · `EVERYONE SAYS YES.` · `SEND FOR KRISHNA.` · `SAKHYA: GOD AS FRIEND.` · then, large: `THE FRIEND WHO SEES FURTHER.`

If you don't, ask what the wisest person you know would see that you're missing.

752.title: What a king is for
752.hook: Krishna answers: a king in Magadha holds kings captive, and a ruler's first duty is to protect
752.carry: raja dharma: a leader's first duty is to protect
752.howItsDone: The Rajasuya belongs to the Vedic royal rites; in the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira's Rajasuya is the rite through which other kings recognize his rule at Indraprastha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: everyone in the sabha said yes, and Yudhishthira sent for Krishna anyway. Your line was krishna, the friend who sees further.

Krishna comes straight from Dwaraka, and Yudhishthira lays it all out. My father's wish. The sacrifice. My ministers say yes, my brothers say yes. But you'll tell me the truth: should I perform the Rajasuya? And Krishna does. You have every quality it takes, he says. Then comes the but. There's a king in Magadha. While he lives, this can't be done.
screen: `KRISHNA COMES.` → `SHOULD I DO THIS?` → `YES. BUT THERE'S A KING IN MAGADHA.`

segments.voice: First, what Yudhishthira is asking for. The Rajasuya is the great royal sacrifice, the one Harishchandra performed. A king who completes it is honored by other kings as sovereign over them, so other rulers have to come, and bow, and bring gifts. That's exactly the problem Krishna names. The king is Jarasandha of Magadha. Many kings already bow to him. Worse, he has captured kings in battle and holds them shut up in his mountain city, meaning to offer them as a sacrifice to Mahadeva. While those kings sit in his prison, Krishna says, no one else can claim to be honored by the kings of the earth. And Krishna tells it as someone hurt by it: fearing Jarasandha, his own people, the Yadavas, left Mathura for Dwaraka. Now look at what his counsel does. Yudhishthira asked, am I worthy of the honor? Krishna answers, what about the people in that prison? That's a teaching the epic comes back to again and again: raja dharma, the dharma of a king. In Hindu teaching, a ruler isn't there to be honored. He's there to protect, above all the ones who can't protect themselves. Jarasandha is the picture of the opposite: a king who uses people, even as offerings. So before anyone can be honored, someone has to be set free. Many teachers read it as a question for anyone who leads, a family, a team, a class: whom are you protecting? Tomorrow, Yudhishthira very nearly gives the whole thing up.

753.title: Born in two halves
753.hook: Yudhishthira wants to give up; Bhima argues for effort, and Krishna tells how Jarasandha was born in two halves
753.carry: daiva and effort: you still do your part
753.howItsDone: The story of Jarasandha's birth is told in the Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata, which Hindus read, hear recited and see performed as part of the epic.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rajasuya ran into a locked gate: Jarasandha, and the kings in his prison. Your line was raja dharma, a leader's first duty is to protect.

Yudhishthira hears about Jarasandha and does something unexpected. He backs down. If even Krishna's people fled from this man, he says, how can we stand against him? Let's give up the sacrifice. Peace is better. It's a startling thing to hear from the man whose father asked for this. Then his brothers speak, one after the other. And Krishna tells a story about how Jarasandha came to be born.
screen: `LET'S GIVE IT UP.` → `THE BROTHERS SPEAK.` → `KRISHNA TELLS A BIRTH STORY.`

segments.voice: Bhima speaks first, and bluntly. A king who never makes an effort, he says, wears down like an anthill. Then a plan: Krishna's wisdom, my strength, Arjuna's skill. Krishna and Arjuna argue for it too. Yudhishthira's caution isn't mocked. It's answered. Hindu thought has names for the two sides of this argument: daiva, what's given, fate, the hand of the gods; and purushakara, human effort. The Mahabharata keeps setting them side by side, and the reading most teachers give is that you need both. You can't control how it turns out, but that never excuses not doing your part. Then Krishna tells where the enemy came from. A king of Magadha named Brihadratha had two wives and no son. A sage, Chandakaushika, gave him a single fruit to bring a son. The king divided it between his two wives, so neither would be left out. Each queen gave birth to half a child: one eye, one arm, one leg each. Horrified, the queens had the halves left outside. A rakshasi named Jara found them, and as she picked them up, the halves joined into one strong child. She carried him back to the king, and in the epic's telling, Magadha held a festival in her honor. The text says his name comes from her: Jarasandha, the one joined by Jara. Even here, the two meet: a sage's gift, a father's fair choice, a stranger's hands. The strength was given to him. What he did with it was his. Tomorrow, the three set out for Magadha, and not dressed as warriors.

754.title: Guests at midnight
754.hook: three men in student dress refuse Jarasandha's welcome; why a host's welcome is sacred in Hindu life
754.carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is god
754.howItsDone: A Hindu host traditionally offers a guest water, a seat and food, and the Taittiriya Upanishad's 'atithi devo bhava', let the guest be God to you, is still taught across India. A snataka is a student who has finished Vedic study and taken the bath that ends it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Rajasuya nearly given up, then Jarasandha's birth in two halves. Your line was daiva and effort: you still do your part.

Three men walk into the capital of Magadha dressed as snatakas, young brahmanas who've just finished their studies. They wear garlands and sandal paste. They don't come in by the main gate, a strange way for students to arrive anywhere. And they walk straight into the king's presence. Jarasandha stands to receive them as honored guests. He has no idea that Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna are standing in his hall.
screen: `DRESSED AS SNATAKAS.` → `NOT BY THE MAIN GATE.` → `THE KING STANDS TO GREET THEM.`

segments.voice: Jarasandha does everything a good host should: water, honors, a seat. They won't take it. Krishna says his two companions are keeping a vow of silence until midnight. So the king leaves, comes back at midnight, and asks what he's been holding. Snatakas don't wear garlands like this. Your arms are marked like the arms of men who draw bows. You came in by a wrong way, and you refused my worship. Who are you? Krishna answers carefully. A snataka enters a friend's house by its gate, and an enemy's by another way. And we don't accept worship from an enemy. Then he names the wrong: you've captured kings to offer them up. We've come to free them. And he tells the king exactly who they are. Why refuse the welcome? Because in Hindu life a host's welcome is close to holy. The Taittiriya Upanishad puts it in a line still taught to children across India: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be God to you. Water, a seat, food: that's how you'd receive a god, and it's how you receive a guest. Many readers say taking that honor binds a guest to his host, so Krishna won't accept it from a man he's come to fight. He'd rather look strange than be false. Jarasandha answers just as plainly. I took those kings in war, and I won't let them go out of fear. Fight me, one of you, or two, or all three. He looks them over, and chooses Bhima.
screen: `THEY REFUSE THE WELCOME.` · `MIDNIGHT: WHO ARE YOU?` · `WE'VE COME TO FREE THEM.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA.` · then, large: `HE CHOOSES BHIMA.`

segments.voice: Hindu homes greet a guest with water first. Before you sit, set out a glass of water as if someone you love were about to walk in. Then close your eyes and picture the next people who'll come through your door, the easy one and the difficult one, and see yourself greeting each as if God had come. If you pray, ask for a welcome that's honest. If you don't, just ask yourself what an honest welcome would look like.

755.title: The prison opens
755.hook: Bhima wrestles Jarasandha for days; Krishna frees the kings and gives the throne to the fallen king's son
755.carry: dharma-vijaya: win to set right, not to take
755.howItsDone: Old Hindu writing on kingship, like the Arthashastra, sets the righteous conqueror, content once the other side yields, against the conqueror who grabs land and wealth; Krishna's handling of Magadha is often told as the picture of a righteous win.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three guests in Jarasandha's hall at midnight, refusing his welcome. Your line was atithi devo bhava, the guest is God.

Jarasandha does one thing first. He has his son, Sahadeva, installed as king, so Magadha won't be left without a ruler. A king who holds other kings in chains still makes sure his own people will have someone on the throne. Then he takes off his crown, binds his hair, and steps out to meet Bhima. No armies, no weapons. Two men, bare-handed, and a crowd of citizens gathering to watch.
screen: `HIS SON MADE KING FIRST.` → `NO ARMIES, NO WEAPONS.` → `BHIMA AND JARASANDHA.`

segments.voice: They wrestle, the text says, without stopping for food or rest, day and night, for days on end. They grip and throw. They strike with arms and knees. At last Jarasandha grows tired, and pauses. Krishna speaks a word to Bhima, who takes it as his signal. He lifts Jarasandha high, whirls him around, and brings him down, and the king of Magadha dies. Here the story could turn into a conquest. It doesn't. The three go straight to the prison and open it. The captive kings walk out and ask Krishna, what can we do for you? His answer is small: Yudhishthira wants to perform the Rajasuya. Help him. That's all. Then Jarasandha's son, Sahadeva, comes out with his ministers, bowing low, offering gifts. Magadha is theirs for the taking, and Krishna gives it back. He reassures the young man and installs him as king, on his father's throne. Old Hindu writing on kingship has a name for this kind of win: dharma-vijaya, a righteous victory. There, the righteous conqueror is content once the other side yields; he doesn't grab its land or its family. Krishna goes further still: he frees the captives, asks only for help with the sacrifice, and leaves the defeated family their home. Many teachers read the scene this way: in Hindu eyes, how you win is part of whether you were right. A victory that grabs everything just makes the winner the next Jarasandha.

segments.voice: There's a Sanskrit prayer many Hindus say: lokah samastah sukhino bhavantu, may all beings everywhere be happy. Bring to mind someone you came out ahead of, in an argument, a game or a contest, and say it for them, slowly, a few times. If you don't pray, simply wish them well in your own words, and think of one real thing you could leave them or give back.

756.title: Arjuna at the northern gate
756.hook: the four brothers ride to the four directions; at the edge of the world, Arjuna keeps a sacred limit
756.carry: maryada: some ground you don't take
756.howItsDone: The word digvijaya, conquest of the directions, outlived the epic: tradition uses it for the travels of the teacher Shankara, whose victories are told as debates won across India rather than battles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the road to the Rajasuya, a prison opened and Jarasandha's son was put on his father's throne. Your line was dharma-vijaya, win to set right, not to take.

Back at Indraprastha, the plan gets bigger. If kings are going to honor Yudhishthira, the brothers will have to go and meet them first. So the younger four divide the world. Arjuna rides north. Bhima rides east. Sahadeva rides south. Nakula rides west. Yudhishthira stays home in the hall, with Dhaumya and his friends around him. Each brother will come back with the tribute of kings. And one will come back from a place where there was nothing to win.
screen: `NORTH, EAST, SOUTH, WEST.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA STAYS HOME.` → `A PLACE WITH NOTHING TO WIN.`

segments.voice: The text follows each brother in turn: kingdoms, battles, and kings who submit or welcome them and send gifts. But one moment at the northern edge stands apart. Arjuna rides on, past mountain after mountain, to the land of the Northern Kurus. At the gate, powerful guards stop him, and they speak kindly. You can't conquer this place, they say. Even if you came in, you couldn't see anything with human eyes. We're pleased with you. Tell us what you want. And Arjuna doesn't push. I want my brother to be sovereign, he says. If this land is closed to humans, I won't enter. Give something as tribute, and I'll go. They give him fine cloth, ornaments and skins, and he turns back. The greatest archer of his age, who won Draupadi with his bow, meets a boundary and keeps it. Hindus have a word for that: maryada, the right limit, the line you don't cross even when you could. It's why Rama is called maryada purushottama, the best of men, who kept the bounds. And it's built into ordinary worship. Shoes come off at the temple door. Many people touch the step before they go in. And the inner shrine, the garbhagriha, where the murti sits, is in many temples for the priests alone; everyone else takes darshan from just outside. Holy ground is entered asking, not taking. This week ran from a father's message to a prison opened and four brothers coming home with the world's gifts. Tomorrow, the Rajasuya itself.
